title: Waiting for Permission
author: Becky Abrams Wilmoth
summary: Becky Abrams Wilmoth reflects on the evolving reality of 'permissionless education' — hybrid schools, microschools, and other innovative models operating outside conventional regulatory frameworks — and argues that the movement has matured from fringe experiment to established wave whose precedents are now reshaping regulatory classification. Writing as a hybrid school founder and consultant since 2019, she tracks her own journey from skepticism about permissionless framing (confronted early on by property-tax exemptions, fire marshal compliance, and OSHA requirements) to witnessing its expanding institutional footprint at the fifth National Hybrid Schools Project Conference in April 2026. The article's conceptual anchor is business professor Robert Randolph's observation that 'policy is always backward-facing' — regulatory frameworks classify and legitimise what already exists rather than enabling what hasn't yet. Abrams Wilmoth illustrates this with a concrete case: a Kansas nonprofit she was consulting received two rejections for sales tax exemption because regulators said 'you're not a school, you're not a church, we don't know what to do with you'; a week later, the Kansas Department of Revenue created a new classification — 'nonsectarian comprehensive multidiscipline youth organisation' — and approved the exemption with an apology. She documents this precedent specifically to use it for future founders in Kansas facing the same barrier. The article describes a wave of similar institutional legitimisation: public schools hosting microschools in their buildings, failing schools reconstituted as parent-led microschools, private schools adding hybrid tracks with accredited diplomas.
points: The 'backward-facing policy' framework offers innovative education founders a practical operating principle: build the model, document it clearly, and let regulatory vocabulary catch up to precedents already established rather than waiting for permission that doesn't yet have language to describe what is being requested.

The Kansas tax-exemption case illustrates the dynamic precisely: two rejections due to absent regulatory category, followed by a self-created new category ('nonsectarian comprehensive multidiscipline youth organisation') that can now serve as precedent for subsequent founders facing identical classification barriers.

The fifth National Hybrid Schools Project Conference in 2026 signals that the hybrid and microschool movement has moved from experimental fringe to established and growing sector, with programmes appearing inside public school buildings, as privately-led reconstitutions of failing schools, and as hybrid tracks within traditional private schools.

Documenting regulatory precedents in one jurisdiction — as Abrams Wilmoth does with the Kansas case — creates replicable pathways that reduce friction for subsequent founders, effectively turning individual compliance victories into institutional infrastructure for the movement.

The tension between operating permissionlessly and compliance requirements is real and ongoing; the author's own hybrid programme navigated property-tax exemptions, fire codes, and OSHA requirements, suggesting the 'permissionless' frame describes an orientation toward innovation rather than literal immunity from regulatory engagement.
quotes: I first heard this term when I attended the 1st Annual National Hybrid Schools Project Conference in 2022. I'll admit—I was skeptical. Maybe it's my conservative Southern Baptist upbringing… or my West Coast mentality...where one must ask for permission from the government for pretty much everything.
I remember hearing the term come up multiple times after the conference as well from well-known voices like Kerry McDonald and Don Soifer and thinking, 'We'll see….'

Fast forward to April 2026 where, after a two-year hiatus of my own, I again attended the National Hybrid Schools Project Conference—the 5th annual. I already knew 'permissionless education' was catching on in part due to my own work with new founders and the fact that it was increasing—not decreasing. I was pleasantly surprised, however, to see at the conference just how much the movement is growing and how established these programs are becoming.

Robert shifted gears to home in on the permissionless elements that we are confronted with daily in this space. At one point, Robert said, 'Policy is always backward facing…' and that stuck with me…and apparently others as another attendee, Heidi Fritz from Heart Christian Academy, brought it up to me again last week—commenting that his statement stuck with her as well.
Their response was along the lines of 'You're not a school…you're not a church…we don't know what to do with you…' Sounds familiar!

A week later, out of the blue, they sent her a personal email stating that after further discussion with the Kansas Dept of Revenue legal team, they had decided to classify their organization as a 'nonsectarian comprehensive multidiscipline youth organization.' A mouthful! They apologized for confusion and approved the exemption request.

I have a handful of founders that I am working with in Kansas and I am documenting this particular case so that we can use it as the precedent for other nonprofits requesting exemption in the near future. And just like that…the policy is backward facing.
